echoes.note: Formula-cited ('Well did Isaiah prophesy of you'). Mt 15:8-9 reproduces Isaiah's indictment of lip-service worship ('this people draw near with their mouth... but their heart is far from me... in vain do they worship, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men'). Verbatim LXX-leaning quotation; the climactic charge of the pericope.
'Honor your father and your mother' cited verbatim as 'the commandment of God' (Mt 15:4), the fifth word of the Decalogue, set against the Corban evasion.
Parallel Decalogue form of 'Honor your father and mother'; Jesus' citation may carry the Deuteronomic as well as Exodus wording. Same commandment, recurrence reinforces.
'He who speaks evil of (curses) father or mother, let him be put to death' cited verbatim (Mt 15:4b) as the sanction backing the fifth commandment.
Holiness-code parallel to Ex 21:17: 'Everyone who curses his father or mother shall surely be put to death.' Likely conflated in Jesus' citation; recurrence strengthens the death-penalty backing.
'Cursed is he who dishonors his father or mother' — the Shechem covenant curse echoing the same dishonor/honor logic Jesus invokes against the Corban tradition.

Law of vows: 'If a man vows a vow to the LORD... he shall not break his word.' Underlies the Corban ('a gift devoted to God') practice Jesus targets — a binding vow weaponized against the fifth commandment.
Legislation on things 'devoted' (qorban/herem) to the LORD; the technical 'gift devoted to God' (Mt 15:5) draws on this dedicatory vocabulary.
Vows to the LORD must be paid and not delayed — the legal background that made Corban vows seem inviolable, which Jesus exposes as a pretext.
'Whoever curses his father or mother, his lamp will be put out' — wisdom restatement of the dishonor sanction echoed in Mt 15:4.
The generation that curses its father and does not bless its mother; thematic resonance with the dishonor Jesus condemns.
'You are near in their mouth and far from their heart' — close conceptual parallel to Isaiah 29:13's mouth/heart contrast that Jesus quotes; reinforces the lip-vs-heart motif.
'With their mouth they show much love, but their heart goes after gain' — same prophetic indictment of mouth-honoring without the heart, paralleling the quoted Isaiah 29:13.
'Every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil' — anthropological root of Jesus' claim that defilement proceeds from the heart, source of 'evil thoughts' (Mt 15:19).
'The imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth' — reinforces the heart-as-source-of-evil premise underlying 15:18-19.
'The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick' — prophetic anthropology directly behind 'out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders...' (Mt 15:19).
The catalogue of vices (murders, adulteries, thefts, false testimony) in Mt 15:19 follows the order of the second table of the Decalogue, casting heart-evil as Decalogue-breaking.
Deuteronomic Decalogue parallel to the Mt 15:19 vice list (murder, adultery, theft, false witness).

'They are the branch of my planting, the work of my hands' — God's true planting language behind 'every plant my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted' (Mt 15:13); the Pharisees are not God's planting.
The Song of the Vineyard: God's planting that fails and is destroyed — background to the uprooting of every plant not planted by the Father.
Prophetic commission 'to pluck up and to plant' — the plucking/planting polarity Jesus invokes in 15:13.
'Oaks of righteousness, the planting of the LORD' — God's planting motif resonant with Mt 15:13.
'Who is blind but my servant... blind as the LORD's messenger?' — prophetic 'blind' leadership behind 'blind guides of the blind' (Mt 15:14).
'His watchmen are blind, they are all without knowledge' — blind Israelite leaders, a strong source for the 'blind guides' charge.
'The leaders of this people cause them to err, and those led are destroyed' — guides leading the people to ruin, paralleling both falling into the pit (15:14).
'Whoever digs a pit will fall into it' — wisdom topos of falling into the pit echoed in 'both will fall into a pit' (Mt 15:14).

'Hear but do not understand... lest they understand with their heart' — the hearing/understanding/heart cluster ironically inverted in Jesus' 'Hear and understand' (15:10) and the disciples' dullness (15:16).
'Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it are the springs of life' — heart as the wellspring from which everything proceeds, paralleling 'out of the heart come...' (15:18-19).

'My sheep were scattered... they wandered, lost.' Jesus' mission 'to the lost sheep of the house of Israel' (Mt 15:24) draws directly on Ezekiel's scattered/lost flock that God himself will seek and shepherd.
'My people have been lost sheep; their shepherds have led them astray' — close verbal source for 'the lost sheep of the house of Israel' (Mt 15:24).
'All we like sheep have gone astray' — the lost/straying sheep image behind 15:24.
'I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek your servant' — individual lost-sheep language resonant with Mt 15:24.
The Davidic covenant promising an eternal son/throne — basis for the Gentile woman's address 'Lord, you son of David' (Mt 15:22), a messianic title.
'A shoot from the stump of Jesse' — Davidic-messianic hope behind the 'son of David' acclamation in 15:22.

Elijah sent to the Gentile widow of Zarephath, in the region of Sidon, whose son he heals — a typological precedent for Jesus in 'the region of Tyre and Sidon' (15:21) granting mercy and healing to a Gentile woman's child.
'Israel is my son, my firstborn' — Israel's status as God's children illumines 'the children's bread' (Mt 15:26) reserved first for Israel before Gentiles.
'You are the children of the LORD your God' — Israel as God's children, background to the children-vs-dogs (Israel-vs-Gentiles) contrast of 15:26.
Rahab the Canaanite who confesses Israel's God and is saved — a figural precedent for a Canaanite woman whose faith Jesus praises (Mt 15:28); Matthew has already named Rahab in the genealogy.
The curse on Canaan to be servant — the Canaanite woman's reversal (faith commended) stands against the Canaanite-as-cursed-outsider background flagged by Matthew's pointed label 'a Canaanite woman'.

'Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, the ears of the deaf unstopped; the lame man shall leap, and the tongue of the mute sing.' Mt 15:30-31's catalogue of mute speaking, lame walking, blind seeing reproduces Isaiah's portrait of eschatological restoration almost item for item.

'The deaf shall hear... the eyes of the blind shall see... the meek shall obtain fresh joy' — recurrence with the Isaiah 29 already quoted in 15:8-9 binds the chapter; the healings fulfill the same oracle.
'They will sanctify... the God of Israel' — the crowd's response 'they glorified the God of Israel' (15:31) echoes Isaiah 29's promised honoring of Israel's God, reversing the lip-service of 15:8-9.
'Who makes the mute, the deaf, the seeing, or the blind? Is it not I, the LORD?' — the divine prerogative over these very disabilities, now exercised by Jesus, prompting glory to 'the God of Israel'.
Jesus 'went up into the mountain, and sat there' (15:29) before the crowds and the feeding — a faint Sinai/Moses-on-the-mountain coloring.
'The LORD opens the eyes of the blind; the LORD raises up those who are bowed down' — the God of Israel as healer of these conditions, glorified in 15:31.

The manna in the wilderness: God feeds a vast multitude in a 'deserted place' (Mt 15:33) where there is nothing to eat, and all 'ate and were filled' (15:37). The feeding of the four thousand is patterned on the wilderness provision.

Elisha feeds a hundred men with a few loaves, who 'ate and had some left over' — the closest prophetic precedent: limited loaves, a doubting servant ('how can I set this before a hundred?'), eating to satisfaction, and leftovers, all mirrored in 15:34-37.

'Can God spread a table in the wilderness?... he rained down manna... they ate and were well filled.' The doubting question of 15:33 and the satisfied eating of 15:37 echo this recital of the wilderness feeding.

Moses' concern that the congregation not be 'as sheep without a shepherd' — behind Jesus' compassion on the hungry multitude (15:32) he refuses to send away; pastoral provision for a leaderless flock.
God the shepherd will feed his flock in good pasture and seek the lost — recurrence with 15:24's lost sheep; the feeding enacts the shepherd's provision of food.

The hungry and thirsty fainting in the wilderness whom God satisfies: 'he satisfies the longing soul, and fills the hungry with good things' — resonant with the fainting-on-the-way concern and the filling of 15:32-37.
'You prepare a table before me' — the shepherd providing a meal, faint background to the wilderness feeding.
'You shall eat and be full, and you shall bless the LORD' — the eat-and-be-satisfied formula echoed in 'they all ate, and were filled' (15:37), with Jesus giving thanks.
'You open your hand and satisfy the desire of every living thing' — God satisfying the hungry, faint resonance with the multitude filled in 15:37.
